title: Adenomyosis and Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB-A)—Pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management
journal: Best Practice & Research Clinical Obstetrics and Gynaecology
article_subtype: Clinical review of adenomyosis etiology, diagnosis, and management
clinical_background: Adenomyosis is a structural cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in the FIGO PALM-COIEN classification. Its prevalence is difficult to establish because confirmation has generally relied on histology, while diagnostic definitions remain disputed. Increasing use of transvaginal ultrasound and MRI has improved noninvasive diagnosis. Pain and heavy menstrual bleeding are prominent presentations, although the relationship between adenomyosis and bleeding remains debated. Evidence also increasingly suggests effects on spontaneous pregnancy and assisted reproduction. Treatment aims to relieve symptoms and preserve fertility when desired; hysterectomy is not suitable for every woman.
objectives: Describe how adenomyosis can be diagnosed in current clinical practice.
Critically assess management options, identifying currently acceptable treatments and areas needing further study.
study_design: Review chapter examining the etiology, diagnosis, and management of adenomyosis and critically appraising treatment options.
interpretation: The authors describe adenomyosis as a condition with several possible pathogenic pathways, particularly processes involving injury and repair at the endometrial–myometrial junction; its causes are not fully established. Symptoms alone do not reliably identify the disease, whereas contemporary imaging can support an accurate noninvasive diagnosis. Treatment choice depends on bleeding, pain, fertility goals and whether uterine preservation is desired. LNG-IUD has the most evidence among medical options, although that evidence is not strong. Hysterectomy is highly effective when future fertility is not desired; uterine-preserving surgery and image-guided interventions offer alternatives, but their comparative and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Adenomyosis may also impair fertility and affect pregnancy outcomes.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier sonographic studies reported poor diagnostic accuracy, whereas studies using newer transvaginal techniques report substantially better performance. A meta-analysis published in 2010 found high accuracy for both ultrasound and MRI but found that MRI more often yielded the correct diagnosis; the authors nevertheless consider ultrasonography performed by well-trained sonographers comparable to MRI in current practice. Evidence on risk factors is inconsistent: studies associating parity or uterine procedures with adenomyosis contrast with retrospective studies finding no association with parity, previous surgery or individual uterine procedures. Reports also disagree about the relationship between heavy menstrual bleeding and adenomyosis, and about its association with endometriosis. Evidence supporting conservative surgery largely comes from small retrospective series rather than randomized trials, while comparative evidence for image-guided interventions is not yet available.
clinical_implications: Neither abnormal uterine bleeding nor pelvic pain distinguishes adenomyosis reliably from other gynecological conditions; symptoms remain relevant to the initial differential diagnosis.
Ultrasound and MRI can permit diagnosis without removing the uterus. Previous endometrial ablation or ongoing medical treatment may reduce imaging accuracy.

For women seeking pregnancy, adenomyosis may adversely affect spontaneous conception, assisted reproduction and obstetric outcomes. A cited case–control study found higher odds of premature delivery (OR 1.84) and premature rupture of membranes (OR 1.98) among women with adenomyosis.
A cited IVF/ICSI meta-analysis reported clinical pregnancy in 123/304 (41%) women with adenomyosis versus 628/1262 (50%) without it, and miscarriage in 77/241 (32%) versus 97/687 (14%), respectively.

After fertility-preserving surgery, residual myometrial thickness may matter: a cited study reported uterine rupture in 2/23 (10%) operated women and identified thickness <8 mm as a possible risk factor.
practice_implications: Prefer a noninvasive diagnostic approach; local availability and expertise may guide the choice between ultrasonography and MRI.
Match treatment to the presenting symptoms and the woman's fertility and uterine-preservation goals.

Consider symptomatic or hormonal medical treatment where appropriate. LNG-IUD is the best-studied medical option discussed, but the supporting evidence is not strong; duration of benefit matters when selecting medical treatment.
For women who do not want future fertility and wish to have the uterus removed, hysterectomy is the definitive option described by the authors.

Uterine-preserving surgery requires substantial surgical expertise, and its reported clinical outcomes rest on low-quality evidence. Image-guided sonographic or radiological treatment is an alternative for uterine preservation, but comparative data are unavailable.
Clinicians and women with adenomyosis should be aware of the reported increased risks of premature delivery and premature rupture of membranes.
limitations: Prevalence estimates are uncertain because confirmation commonly relies on histology after hysterectomy, while imaging and pathological diagnostic criteria vary between settings and pathologists.
There is no universally adopted adenomyosis classification system, and the histological depth required for diagnosis remains disputed.

Studies of medical treatments other than LNG-IUD include few women in high-quality research and lack adequate comparisons; evidence for commonly used symptomatic options is limited specifically for adenomyosis.
Conservative surgical outcome data are mostly drawn from small retrospective series rather than randomized trials.

Evidence for sonographic and radiological interventions is largely retrospective. The limited randomized trials chiefly assess adjuncts to an intervention rather than compare techniques, and comparative outcome data are unavailable.
No investigated diagnostic biomarker is currently in use; reported biomarker findings are nonspecific or preliminary.
open_questions: Whether adenomyosis and endometriosis are separate conditions or belong to a disease continuum remains disputed.
The exact contribution of proposed epigenetic, hormonal, reproductive, vascular and immune pathways to adenomyosis is unresolved.
The relationship between adenomyosis and heavy menstrual bleeding, particularly across disease severity, remains contested.
Agreement is lacking on diagnostic thresholds and a classification that can support clinical care and research.
The comparative effectiveness and long-term morbidity and fertility outcomes of uterine-preserving treatments remain uncertain.
future_directions: Develop a classification for research protocols that uses established noninvasive diagnostic terminology and focuses on women's clinical outcomes.
Conduct methodologically robust comparisons of medical options with other medical and surgical treatments.
Collect prospective, long-term morbidity and fertility outcomes after conservative surgery; a clinical registry may be an initial approach.
Collect prospective, long-term morbidity and fertility outcomes after sonographic and radiological interventions; a clinical registry may likewise be an initial approach.
Pursue higher-quality prospective longitudinal comparisons of conservative surgery and interventional techniques, recognizing that randomized comparisons may not be feasible in the short term.
Investigate reproductive function in untreated women with adenomyosis and in women requiring ART, including whether combined medical treatments can improve outcomes.

tables.title: Definitions of adenomyosis

rows: Uduwela AS, Perera MA, Aiqing L et al. 2000 [32]
Disruption of the usual boundary between the endometrium and myometrium.
Bazot M, Cortez A, Darai E et al. 2001 [33]
Basal-type, nonsecretory ectopic endometrium directly connected to the eutopic basalis.
Based on thickness
Vercellini P, Ragni G, Trespidi L et al. 1993 [34]
Myometrial invasion > 4 mm (one low-power field).
Zaloudek C & Norris HJ. 1987 [35]
Myometrial invasion > 2.5 mm (half a low-power field).
Sanberg EG & Cohn F. 1962 [36]
Myometrial invasion > 8 mm (two low-power fields).
Based on proportion
Hendrickson MR & Kempson RL. 1987 [37]
Invasion involving >1/3 of uterine muscular thickness.
Ferenczy A. 1998 [30]
A distance >25% of uterine muscular thickness between the endometrialemyometrial junction and the nearest adenomyotic focus.

tables.summary: The cited definitions differ in whether they require disruption of the tissue boundary, continuity with the eutopic basalis, a specified depth of invasion, or a specified proportion of myometrial thickness.

tables.title: Classification systems for adenomyosis

rows: Siegler AM & Camilien L. 1994 [63]
Extent: Grade 1, inner 1/3 myometrium; Grade 2, 2/3 myometrium; Grade 3, entire myometrium. Severity: Grade 1 Mild, histologically 1e3 islets/LPF; Grade 2 Moderate, 4e9 islets; Severe, >10 islets.
Hulka CA, Hall Da, McCarthy K et al. 2002 [64]

1. Mild disease: microscopic foci or involvement confined to the inner 1/3 of the myometrium. 2. Focal disease with focal adenomyomas. 3. Severe or diffuse disease extending into the outer 2/3 of the myometrium or involving the entire uterus.
Sammour A, Pirwany I, Usubutun A et al. 2002 [65]

Hysterectomy specimens classified by penetration: 1. <25%; 2. 25e50%; 3. 51e75%; 4. 75% of myometrial thickness. A penetration ratio, calculated as depth of penetration/myometrial thickness, represents disease extent; spread is assessed by the number of foci per slide.
Vercellini, P et al 2006 [66]

1. Presence >2.5 mm from the endometrialemyometrial junction. 2. Penetration depth: mild, <1/3; moderate, 1/3e2/3; severe, >2/3. 3. Spread/LPF: 1e3 islets, Grade 1; 4e10 islets, Grade 2; >10 islets, Grade 3. 4. Lesion configuration: focal, nodular, or diffuse.
Kishi Y, Suginami H, Kuramori R, et al. 2012 [67]

Four MRI-based subtypes, also considering possible etiology: Type I affects only the inner myometrial layer; Type II affects only the outer layer; Type III comprises isolated adenomyomas unrelated to other structural components; Type IV covers other variations.
Grimbizis et al. 2014 [62]

Clinicalehistological stages: 1. Diffuse endometriosis, with glands and stroma distributed through uterine muscle; 2. Focal adenomyosis, comprising distorted and hypertrophic endometrium and myometrium within the myometrium, subdivided into a circumscribed adenomyoma or a predominantly cystic myometrial lesion; 3. Polypoid adenomyomas, circumscribed endometrial masses containing glands and stroma predominantly composed of smooth muscle; 4. Other forms, including endocervical and retroperitoneal forms.

tables.summary: The proposed systems classify disease by myometrial extent, penetration, number of foci, lesion configuration, MRI appearance, or clinicalehistological pattern. The article states that none has been universally adopted.

Women with adenomyosis and uterine size <12 weeks' gestation received GnRHa until uterine size fell to 10 weeks' gestation, followed by LNG-IUD insertion.
At 12 months after combined treatment, menstrual flow (p < 0.03), dysmenorrhea (p < 0.005), and uterine volume (p < 0.005) had decreased significantly. The LNG-IUD expulsion rate was 14%.

LNG-IUD insertion in women with dysmenorrhea and sonographic adenomyosis.
At three years after insertion, dysmenorrhea remained significantly lower (p < 0.001) and uterine volume was reduced relative to baseline. Overall satisfaction was 72%.

HMB and uterine volume decreased significantly, with symptom improvement lasting up to 3 years after insertion. The volume reduction might not appear until 2 years after insertion.

Women with sonographically diagnosed endometriosis treated with dienogest.

tables.summary: The table brings together randomized, prospective, and retrospective reports on medical treatment. Its Ozdegirmenci row lists 75 participants, although its displayed group counts are [42] and [32]. The Nagata treatment cell describes endometriosis, whereas its outcome addresses discontinuation of treatment for adenomyosis; these discrepancies are present in the article.

tables.title: Sonographic and interventional radiological techniques for treating adenomyosis

columns: Treatment(s) studied and number in each group (n)
rows: Randomized controlled trials
Dexamethasone 10 mg + UAE for adenomyosis [30]; UAE alone for adenomyosis [29].
Pain scores differed statistically at 12 and 24 hours post treatment (maximum 2 points on an 11-point VAS); nausea and vomiting were reduced in the dexamethasone group.
Zhang, X., et al. (2014) [91]
USgHIFU treatment of adenomyosis [42]; USgHIFU treatment with oxytocin infusion [42].
In this double-blind RCT, adding oxytocin significantly reduced sonication time and nonperfused volume. Short-term complication rates did not differ, and clinical outcomes were not reported.
Prospective studies
Ferrari, F., et al. (2016) [92]
MRgFUS for symptomatic adenomyosis; diffuse disease [7]; focal disease [11].
Uterine volume decreased for most women; at 1 year post treatment, junctional zone thickness was <12 mm in 15/18 (83%).
USgHIFU for symptomatic adenomyosis with uterine volumes >200 cm3.
Uterine volume and adenomyotic lesions decreased significantly (p < 0.01). Dysmenorrhea showed a significant, sustained reduction at 12 months (p < 0.01), and quality-of-life measures improved.
Retrospective
USgHIFU for symptomatic adenomyosis.

Follow-up was available for 208/230 (90%) women; 71% reported no symptoms. Greater nonperfused volume or older age was associated with a higher likelihood of clinical success, while 26% reported recurrent dysmenorrhea after treatment.
USgHIFU for symptomatic adenomyosis.

Treatment succeeded in 2411/2549 (95%) women; the mean volume ablation rate was 73% (range 21e100%). Adverse events occurred in 10%, predominantly minor abdominal pain and vaginal discharge; major morbidity was rare.
Liang, E., et al. (2012) [96]
UAE for symptomatic adenomyosis.
Dysmenorrhea decreased in 75%, pain resolved in 56%, and uterine volume decreased by 50% after treatment.
Smeets, A. J., et al. (2012) [97]
UAE for symptomatic adenomyosis.
After median follow-up of 58 months (range 38e129 months), 7/40 (18%) underwent hysterectomy for persistent symptoms; 29/40 (72%) had no symptoms and reported significantly improved quality of life.
Short-term outcomes after MRgFUS for symptomatic adenomyosis.
At 6 months post treatment, pain and quality-of-life assessments showed significantly fewer symptoms and better quality of life.
Short-term follow-up after UAE for symptomatic adenomyosis.
At 3e4 months post treatment, 95% reported improvement in dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding; mean uterine volume decreased by 32%.

tables.summary: The studies report symptom, uterine-volume, and quality-of-life outcomes after UAE, USgHIFU, or MRgFUS; the randomized comparisons examine adjunctive dexamethasone or oxytocin rather than comparing the principal techniques. The Zhang row states 86 participants but displays [42] in each treatment group.

main_conclusion: Adenomyosis can be diagnosed reliably without invasive testing, while treatment selection depends on symptoms and whether uterine preservation or future pregnancy is desired. LNG-IUD has the strongest medical-treatment evidence presented, hysterectomy is highly successful when uterine removal is acceptable, and conservative surgery and image-guided interventions remain constrained by limited-quality or noncomparative outcome data.
narrative_summary: This clinical review examines the pathogenesis, diagnosis, classification, and treatment of adenomyosis associated with abnormal uterine bleeding, pain, and subfertility. It draws on published epidemiological, diagnostic, treatment, and reproductive studies rather than reporting a new patient cohort. Histological prevalence estimates vary substantially because diagnostic definitions and the populations undergoing hysterectomy differ. Symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis. In a cited meta-analysis of 23 studies involving 2312 women, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 72% and 81% for ultrasound, compared with 77% and 89% for MRI; the authors favor noninvasive diagnosis, with local expertise informing imaging choice. No proposed classification system has been universally adopted. Treatment is guided by symptoms and fertility goals. LNG-IUD is the best-studied medical option, although the evidence remains limited; a cited longer-term study reported 72% satisfaction. Hysterectomy prevents further bleeding and recurrence when future fertility is not desired. Conservative surgery and sonographic or radiological interventions offer uterine-preserving alternatives, but many reported outcomes come from small or retrospective studies, and comparative evidence is lacking. Reproductive effects also warrant attention: a cited IVF/ICSI meta-analysis reported clinical pregnancy in 123/304 (41%) women with adenomyosis versus 628/1262 (50%) without it, and miscarriage in 77/241 (32%) versus 97/687 (14%). The review calls for stronger comparative treatment studies and prospective long-term morbidity and fertility data.

document_sections.heading: Adenomyosis and Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB-A)dPathogenesis, diagnosis, and management
document_sections.content: Adenomyosis has a complex origin and varied presentation, making it particularly difficult to identify and manage within the FIGO PALM-COIEN abnormal uterine bleeding group. Its prevalence is hard to establish because confirmation commonly relies on histology. Greater access to transvaginal ultrasound and MRI, together with improved accuracy, has made noninvasive diagnosis highly accurate. Pain, abnormal uterine bleeding, and subfertility are the main presentations. Increasing evidence indicates that adenomyosis can impair fecundity and assisted reproduction. Treatment aims to relieve symptoms and improve fertility options. Hysterectomy may be unwanted or inappropriate, especially as women increasingly have children in their fourth and fifth decades.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: The FIGO PALM-COIEN system identifies adenomyosis as a structural cause of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB). As with endometriosis, estimating prevalence is difficult because clinical suspicion based on symptoms and imaging generally requires subsequent histological confirmation. Whether adenomyosis is a distinct pathological condition remains disputed: some proposed features, including an irregular endometrial–myometrial junctional zone, also occur in asymptomatic women. Diagnosis has become more frequent over the last 20 years alongside wider use and greater accuracy of transvaginal ultrasound and MRI. Pain and heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) are the principal symptoms, but their relationships with adenomyosis remain contested. Some cited studies found no relationship with HMB, whereas others associated the condition with greater menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhea. Earlier researchers often found no association with infertility, potentially because presentation commonly occurred in the fourth and fifth decades after childbearing. With pregnancy increasingly delayed until those decades, evidence is growing for adverse effects on spontaneous and assisted pregnancy. This chapter examines proposed causes, diagnosis in current practice, and management options, distinguishing accepted approaches from questions requiring further study.

document_sections.heading: Etiology
document_sections.content: The true prevalence of adenomyosis remains uncertain. Published estimates range from a few percent to 70%; many histological series following hysterectomy, involving up to 2000 women, suggest 20e35%. Differences in imaging criteria and variation in histological interpretation between centers and pathologists complicate prevalence estimates. Multiparity and termination of pregnancy are documented risk factors. Increasing parity, regardless of type, and cesarean delivery have been linked to greater risk; a study of 594 women reported an odds ratio of 5 for this association. A larger series of 1334 women found a weaker association, although histological confirmation increased with parity. In the California Teachers Study, a comparison of 951 women with histologically confirmed adenomyosis and 79,495 without disease identified increasing parity and longer estrogen exposure—associated with early menarche, short cycles, and obesity—as risk factors. One proposed explanation is that pregnancy-related disruption of the endometrial–myometrial junction permits glandular growth within the myometrium. A similar explanation has been proposed for associations with curettage, termination of pregnancy, and cesarean delivery. Findings are inconsistent: a retrospective study of 549 women with histological adenomyosis found no correlation with parity or prior surgery, while another involving 873 women found no correlation with individual uterine procedures but did observe one when procedures were considered together. The author therefore emphasizes the need for agreed diagnostic criteria and methodologically sound research. Tamoxifen use is another reported risk factor. Cigarette smoking may be protective, potentially through effects on circulating estrogen. Increasing age is considered a reliable risk factor, with greater estrogen exposure proposed as a contributor. Whether adenomyosis and endometriosis are separate conditions or part of a continuum is disputed. Imaging studies support a strong association and proposed shared pathogenic pathways. Conversely, a retrospective hysterectomy study of 594 women found no increased association, although endometriosis might have gone unreported or been removed. In a retrospective study of 959 women undergoing polypectomy, adenomyosis was significantly associated with endometrial polyps (p = 0.016), with a stronger association when endocervical polyps were present (p = 0.002). Differences in disease definition further affect epidemiological findings. A histological diagnosis requires endometrial or endometrium-like structures within the myometrium together with smooth muscle hypertrophy or hyperplasia. Definitive assessment entails surgery that a woman may not want; biopsy can miss lesions. Although myometrial glands and stroma are generally accepted features, the required depth below the eutopic endometrium is disputed. Apparent depth can vary with specimen sectioning and natural irregularity of the endometrial–myometrial border. Requiring a direct connection between ectopic tissue and the eutopic basalis is also controversial because isolated deep myometrial cystic lesions have been documented. Table 1 presents differing definitions. Several possible pathogenic mechanisms may coexist. A frequently proposed mechanism is inward folding and direct invasion of endometrium into myometrium. Potential disruption of the interface through pregnancy, myometrial incisions, leiomyomas, and age-related injury and repair has increasing supporting evidence. MMPs and TIMPs have been implicated in basement membrane injury; VEGF, cyclooxygenase, and stem cell progenitors have also been proposed as contributors to disease initiation, persistence, or progression. Vascular involvement has been suggested: one pathological study identified adenomyosis in 54/434 (12%) histologically examined uterine blood vessels, raising possibilities of local or more distant spread and initiation by multipotential perivascular cells. Dysmenorrhea is common, and oxytocin receptors may be more abundant in affected women than in those without adenomyosis. Proposed immune mechanisms include lymphocyte proliferation and antibody formation leading to tissue injury and glandular infiltration. Reported macrophage effects on endometrial stromal cells, followed by increased interleukin production, may contribute to implants and offer a future route for immunogenic treatment. Despite theories linking adenomyosis with other benign reproductive conditions, including endometriosis and leiomyomas, the roles of epigenetic, hormonal, and reproductive factors remain incompletely understood.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Histology is the definitive diagnostic approach, though its necessity is debated and the required depth of myometrial invasion varies. Disagreement about acceptable criteria impedes classification for research and clinical management. Complete assessment of the myometrium requires major surgery, which may be unacceptable; hysterectomy is not an option when current or future fertility is desired. For a woman presenting primarily with HMB, hysterectomy could both establish a diagnosis and treat bleeding, even if adenomyosis is not confirmed histologically. Less invasive histological sampling methods have been developed, but their performance has been described as high in sensitivity and low in specificity. In a prospective study of 102 women undergoing hysterectomy after ultrasound-guided needle biopsy, examination of the entire uterus confirmed adenomyosis in 29/102 (28%). TVUS sensitivity was 83% and biopsy sensitivity was 45%; their respective specificities were 67% and 96%. Combining them did not improve diagnostic performance, and the study authors judged both tests to have shortcomings. In a prospective laparoscopic evaluation of 72 women using one full-thickness uterine needle biopsy, adenomyosis was identified in 8/42 (19%) women with dysmenorrhea and 5/30 (17%) asymptomatic women. These findings suggested no diagnostic advantage for that technique.

document_sections.heading: Ultrasound and MRI
document_sections.content: Imaging can diagnose adenomyosis without surgery. A recent consensus statement sets out terminology, definitions, and measurements for describing uterine disease sonographically, offering a basis for consistent research terminology. Diagnostic accuracy must be interpreted in light of changing technology: early sonography studies reported poor performance, whereas improvements in 2D transvaginal ultrasound have been followed by studies reporting very high accuracy. In a prospective study of 54 symptomatic women scheduled for hysterectomy, 3D ultrasound mapped suspected lesions before guided full-thickness biopsies from serosa to endometrium. Sensitivity was 92%, specificity 83%, PPV 99%, and NPV 71%. Previous endometrial ablation or ongoing medical treatment substantially reduced accuracy, potentially because these alter the endometrial–myometrial interface. In another prospective study, 72 women underwent 2D and 3D TVS before hysterectomy, and histology identified adenomyosis in 32/72 (44%). Myometrial cysts were the most specific 2D TVS feature, while heterogeneous myometrium was the most sensitive. For 2D and 3D TVS, respectively, overall accuracy was 83% and 89%, sensitivity 75% and 91%, specificity 90% and 88%, positive predictive value 86% and 85%, and negative predictive value 82% and 92%. These results came from expert sonologists applying closely specified criteria and rigorous methods, illustrating the accuracy attainable in expert practice. Comparisons of ultrasound with MRI must likewise account for changes over time. A prospective series from 2001 involving 106 women found greater specificity for MRI than ultrasound but similar sensitivity. MRI may be more accurate and is less operator-dependent, yet it is substantially more expensive and less accessible than transvaginal ultrasound. A meta-analysis published in 2010 pooled 23 studies involving 2312 women and found high noninvasive diagnostic accuracy for both methods, with MRI more often providing the correct diagnosis. Pooled ultrasound sensitivity and specificity were 72% and 81%; MRI sensitivity and specificity were 77% and 89%. Preliminary reports suggest that elastography, which evaluates tissue strain sonographically, may improve ultrasound accuracy, but evidence remains limited. Improved imaging and interpretation support high diagnostic accuracy with either ultrasound or MRI. Local availability and expertise may determine the choice, and standardized imaging reports could underpin future classification systems.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: Symptoms alone are neither sensitive nor specific for diagnosing adenomyosis, although the clinical presentation should inform the initial differential diagnosis. Women may present with AUB, pelvic pain, or infertility. HMB does not appear strongly predictive across all forms of adenomyosis, though more severe disease may make it more likely. Dysmenorrhea also occurs in other gynecological conditions; cited studies describe it in adenomyosis but provide no pain characteristics that distinguish adenomyosis from endometriosis or leiomyomas.

document_sections.heading: Biomarkers
document_sections.content: Investigated diagnostic biomarkers have been less successful than imaging, and none is currently used. Many relate to proposed causes of disease but lack specificity for distinguishing adenomyosis from other gynecological or systemic disorders. MALDI-TOF MS has been proposed as a possible diagnostic approach for adenomyosis and endometriosis, but it cannot distinguish between them. Myosin has been reported to be overexpressed in adenomyosis and might help assess the extent of myometrial disease; these findings remain preliminary.

document_sections.heading: Classification
document_sections.content: Reviews, studies, and consensus meetings have called for an adenomyosis classification system to support diagnosis, shared management planning, and research. Several systems have been proposed, but none has gained universal acceptance, creating difficulties in both practice and research. Table 2 outlines the proposed systems.

document_sections.heading: Treatment
document_sections.content: Treatment selection depends on whether pain, AUB, or infertility is present. Options include medical treatment, surgery, radiological or sonographic interventions, and combinations of these approaches.

document_sections.heading: Medical treatment
document_sections.content: Medical therapies are often used first. NSAIDs and the combined oral contraceptive pill are frequently used for AUB, but evidence on outcomes specifically attributable to adenomyosis is sparse. LNG-IUD is the most extensively studied medical treatment. An RCT assigning 75 women to the device or hysterectomy found equivalent bleeding outcomes over short-term follow-up and a small advantage for LNG-IUD in some quality-of-life measures. Larger and longer-term data reported 72% satisfaction with LNG-IUD. It can relieve symptoms, reduce uterine volume, and preserve the possibility of later pregnancy, making it a reasonable option for many affected women. GnRHa, danazol, oral progestins, and aromatase inhibitors have also been reported as effective, but high-quality studies include few women and comparative evidence is currently lacking. Retaining the uterus permits pregnancy after treatment. Table 3 summarizes adenomyosis-specific medical-treatment studies by study design.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Treatment
document_sections.content: Surgical options include excision or cytoreduction intended to preserve fertility; endometrial ablation when fertility is not intended, after which pregnancy is contraindicated; and removal of the entire uterus. Hysterectomy stops bleeding and eliminates recurrence, and is the gold-standard treatment when future fertility is not desired. Endometrial–myometrial resection has reportedly succeeded, with invasion depth affecting prognosis. In a prospective series of 50 women, outcomes were uniformly good for superficial disease but failure was frequent in deep disease. A retrospective study of 190 women found that GnRHa before rollerball ablation did not significantly alter outcomes; ablation with or without medical therapy significantly reduced both AUB-A and dysmenorrhea. Fertility-preserving hysteroscopic excision of cystic lesions has also been reported but demands substantial surgical skill. Conservative surgery intended to maintain or improve fertility is particularly challenging. A cited meta-analysis involving 1049 women reported that complete excision reduced dysmenorrhea by 82% and HMB by 69%, with a pregnancy rate of 60%. Following partial excision, the respective figures were 82%, 50%, and 47%. More extensive disease may have made partial excision more common and contributed to worse outcomes. None of these data came from randomized trials; most studies were small retrospective series. Fertility-sparing operations require considerable expertise. Temporary uterine artery occlusion has been reported to reduce bleeding and technical difficulty. In a retrospective series of 179 women treated with laparoscopic uterine artery occlusion and partial resection, with up to 3 years followup, mean sonographic uterine-volume reduction was 58% at 36 months and quality of life improved significantly. A separate retrospective study of 37 women reported clinical improvement with the same techniques. A 10-year series involving 104 women with extensive disease described a technically demanding triple-flap cytoreduction and reconstruction approach intended to preserve fertility. After surgery, 16/26 (61%) women seeking pregnancy conceived and 14/26 (54%) delivered at term; no uterine rupture was reported. In a preliminary series of 15 women, laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation permitted biopsy of adenomyotic nodules followed by ablation of suspected lesions. Reduced symptoms were reported, but fertility outcomes were not yet available.

document_sections.heading: Radiologic or Sonographic Interventions as Treatment
document_sections.content: High-intensity ultrasound and interventional radiology are increasingly described as nonsurgical options. Most evidence is retrospective, although clinical reports and prospective assessments are accumulating. The limited RCTs chiefly evaluate additions to a principal intervention rather than compare techniques. Table 4 summarizes recent studies and their clinical outcomes. Fertility-related decisions must also account for effects of untreated adenomyosis on spontaneous conception, ART, and pregnancy outcomes after procedures. A large case–control study of 2138 women reported higher odds of premature delivery (OR 1.84) and premature rupture of membranes (OR 1.98) among those with adenomyosis; women and their clinicians should be aware of these risks. Junctional-zone changes may contribute to placentation problems, premature delivery, other major obstetric complications, fetal growth restriction, and poorer neonatal outcomes. Myometrial thickness may influence pregnancy outcome after surgery: uterine rupture occurred in 2/23 (10%) operated women, and thickness of <8 mm may be a risk factor. For IVF, a cited meta-analysis reported significantly lower pregnancy and delivery rates with adenomyosis. Pooled information from 1865 women across four prospective and five retrospective IVF/ICSI studies showed clinical pregnancy in 123/304 (41%) women with adenomyosis versus 628/1262 (50%) without it. Miscarriage occurred in 77/241 (32%) women with adenomyosis and 97/687 (14%) without it; the source also gives 14.1% for the latter group. MRI studies have demonstrated uterotubal disturbance in women with adenomyosis as a likely contributor to subfertility. Dysperistalsis, potentially more frequent in diffuse disease, and greater symptoms may impair sperm transport during spontaneous conception and increase implantation failure during ART.

document_sections.heading: Practice Points
document_sections.content: The proposed complex etiology involves injury and repair at the junctional zone. More menstrual cycles, uterine instrumentation associated with miscarriage, cesarean delivery or surgery, and more deliveries are identified as risk factors. Reliable noninvasive diagnosis is possible and is preferred. In current practice, ultrasonography performed by well-trained sonographers has diagnostic accuracy equal to MRI. Medical care may use straightforward symptomatic measures or hormonal options. LNG-IUD is described as the best-studied and most effective medical option, although its supporting evidence is not strong; expected treatment duration also matters when choosing medical therapy. Conservative surgery demands substantial expertise, and evidence for its clinical outcomes is of low quality. Hysterectomy is highly successful when uterine removal is wanted. Sonographic and radiological interventions may preserve the uterus as alternatives to conservative surgery; evidence supporting their success and safety is emerging, but comparative data are unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Research Agenda
document_sections.content: A classification system suitable for research protocols is needed now that reasonable noninvasive diagnostic methods and descriptive terminology have been established; it should focus on clinical outcomes for women. The author calls for methodologically sound comparisons of medical approaches with other medical and surgical options. Prospective evidence is needed on long-term morbidity and fertility after conservative surgery and after interventional sonographic or radiological treatment; clinical registries might provide an initial approach instead of complex RCTs. Although RCTs comparing conservative surgery with interventional techniques would be ideal, they may not be achievable soon, whereas higher-quality prospective longitudinal research appears feasible. Further work should examine reproductive function both in untreated women with adenomyosis and in those needing ART, particularly whether combined medical treatments could improve outcomes.

main_findings.description: A cited IVF/ICSI meta-analysis reported a lower clinical pregnancy rate among women with adenomyosis than among those without it.
main_findings.context: Pooled data from 1865 women in four prospective and five retrospective studies. The article reports significant reductions in pregnancy and delivery rates but supplies no delivery-rate estimate here.

main_findings.description: The same cited IVF/ICSI meta-analysis reported more miscarriage among women with adenomyosis than among those without it.
main_findings.context: The article gives both (14%) and (14.1%) for the group without adenomyosis; neither figure has been substituted for the other.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Chen, J., et al. (2015): 10% of women treated with USgHIFU experienced an adverse event; most events were minor, and major morbidity was rare.
notable_adverse_events: Chen, J., et al. (2015), USgHIFU: abdominal pain and vaginal discharge were among the predominantly minor adverse events; individual rates were not given.
Kelekci, S., et al. (2012), LNG-IUD: acne occurred more often than in the copper IUD group; no rate was given.
Zhang, P., et al. (2013), GnRHa followed by LNG-IUD: the LNG-IUD expulsion rate was 14%.
Zhang, X., et al. (2014), USgHIFU with versus without oxytocin: no difference in short-term complication rates was reported; rates were not given.
Kim, S. Y., et al. (2016), Dexamethasone plus UAE versus UAE alone: nausea and vomiting were reduced in the Dexamethasone group; rates were not given.
Surgical treatment in a cited pregnancy-outcome study: uterine rupture occurred in 2/23 (10%) women; a myometrial thickness of <8 mm was suggested as a possible risk factor.
Triple-flap fertility-sparing surgery in the cited 10-year series: no uterine rupture was reported.

subgroup_analyses: In the cited 50-woman resection series, outcomes were favorable for superficial adenomyosis but failure rates were high for deep disease.

In the cited 1049-woman surgical meta-analysis, complete removal yielded dysmenorrhea reduction of 82%, HMB reduction of 69%, and pregnancy in 60%; partial excision yielded 82%, 50%, and 47%, respectively. These are results by extent of excision, not randomized treatment comparisons.
In the cited 54-woman imaging study, previous endometrial ablation or concurrent medical treatment substantially lowered the accuracy of sonographically guided diagnosis.
In the cited retrospective USgHIFU series of 230 women, higher nonperfused volume or older age was linked to a greater likelihood of clinical success.
The cited prospective MRgFUS series of 18 women included diffuse disease [7] and focal disease [11], but reported no separate outcomes for these groups.
secondary_results: Cited epidemiological findings differed: some studies associated parity and uterine procedures with adenomyosis, whereas the retrospective studies of 549 and 873 women did not find the same individual associations.
The article describes increasing age and tamoxifen use as reported risk factors; cigarette smoking may be protective. It does not supply effect estimates for these findings.
Elastography has preliminary reports of improved sonographic diagnostic accuracy, but the article characterizes the available data as limited.

Medical treatment with NSAIDs and combined oral contraceptive pill is described as commonly used for AUB, with little evidence specific to adenomyosis outcomes. GnRHa, danazol, oral progestins, and aromatase inhibitors are reported as effective in cited studies, but high-quality studies include few women and comparative data are lacking.

For LNG-IUD, the article reports symptomatic relief, reduced uterine volume, and the possibility of future pregnancy; the cited longer-term satisfaction rate is 72%. It describes LNG-IUD as the best studied medical option while cautioning that the evidence is not strong.

MRI is described as less dependent on the operator and potentially more accurate than transvaginal ultrasound, but substantially more expensive and less available. The article also states that, in current practice with well-trained sonographers, ultrasound has diagnostic accuracy equal to MRI.

Cited MRI studies demonstrate uterotubal disturbance in women with adenomyosis. The article presents dysperistalsis and impaired sperm transport or implantation as possible contributors to reduced fertility, rather than measured effects in this review.
For interventional sonographic and radiological treatments, the article describes the evidence as largely retrospective and notes that comparative data between techniques are not yet available.

key_numeric_data.context: Nulligravid women without endometriosis assessed for adenomyosis using transvaginal ultrasonographic features in a cited study of symptom correlations.
